content.title: Intro to AI Concepts — Reading
content.body:
Artificial Intelligence is the field of building systems that perform tasks normally needing human intelligence, such as understanding language, recognising images and making decisions. Machine learning is a subset where systems learn patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules.

Key points

  • Narrow AI solves one task; general AI (hypothetical) would match human ability broadly.
  • Three learning styles: supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement.
  • Data quality matters as much as the algorithm.
  • AI systems can inherit bias from their training data.

content.title: Search & Optimization — Reading
content.body:
Many AI problems are searches for the best sequence of actions. Uninformed methods such as breadth-first and depth-first search explore blindly, while informed methods like A* use a heuristic estimate of the remaining distance to reach goals faster. Optimisation techniques such as gradient descent search for the best numeric settings.

Key points

  • BFS finds the shortest path in unweighted graphs.
  • A* combines path cost so far with a heuristic estimate.
  • A good heuristic never overestimates the true cost.
  • Gradient descent moves step by step downhill on an error surface.

content.title: Neural Network Basics — Reading
content.body:
A neural network is layers of simple units (neurons). Each neuron multiplies its inputs by weights, adds a bias and passes the result through an activation function such as ReLU or sigmoid. Stacking layers lets the network learn complex patterns like faces or speech.

Key points

  • Input layer receives data, hidden layers transform it, output layer predicts.
  • Weights are the values learned during training.
  • Activation functions add non-linearity - without them the network is just a line.
  • Deeper networks can learn richer features but need more data.

content.title: Model Training — Reading
content.body:
Training adjusts the weights to reduce error. The model makes a prediction, a loss function measures how wrong it was, and backpropagation works out how each weight should change. Data is split into training, validation and test sets so you can detect overfitting - when a model memorises instead of generalises.

Key points

  • Typical split: 70% train, 15% validation, 15% test.
  • Learning rate controls the step size of each update.
  • Overfitting: great training score, poor test score.
  • Regularisation and more data help reduce overfitting.

content.title: Capstone: Build a Classifier — Reading
content.body:
For the capstone you build a simple classifier, for example one that labels flowers or spam emails. Load a dataset, clean it, split it, train a model, then evaluate accuracy and mistakes. Finish by writing a short note explaining what worked and what you would improve.

Key points

  • Start with a simple baseline model.
  • Use a confusion matrix to see which classes get mixed up.
  • Change one thing at a time when tuning.
  • Document your results so others can reproduce them.
